definition: A push button with a locator tone, a tactile arrow and audible or vibrating WALK cues for blind and low-vision pedestrians.
The East German hat-wearing pedestrian signal figure presented by Karl Peglau in 1961.
The standard streetlight receptacle; the 5-position version has 2 dimming contacts and the 7-position version has 4, supporting 0-10 V or DALI dimming.
The standard set of paint colors that tells you what kind of utility is buried under a locate mark, such as red for electric and yellow for gas.
Space beside or under the sidewalk belonging to the adjacent building, often reached through cellar doors.
A trailer- or truck-mounted panel of flashing lights showing drivers which way to merge; required at 40 mph and above per Seattle DOT's MUTCD-based manual.
Sign abbreviation for automatic sprinkler, marking an FDC that feeds sprinklers.
Boston gas company formed by a 1905 merger and renamed Boston Gas in 1955; its initials survive on old gas covers.
The black frame around a signal head; FHWA promotes versions with a 1-3 inch yellow retroreflective border.
The flashing amber globe on a striped pole at a UK zebra crossing.
A survey mark with a precisely known elevation, often a brass or aluminum disk.
A drain grate with transverse rods, spacers or curved vanes so bike wheels can't drop into the slots.
A box at least 10 feet deep at the front of a traffic lane where cyclists wait ahead of cars at a red light.
A crossing point where the sidewalk slopes gently into the street instead of using a distinct ramp; PROWAG allows it in place of a curb ramp.
UK tactile paving of flat bumps at pedestrian crossings: red at controlled crossings, usually buff at uncontrolled ones.
A blue raised reflector placed by the center line on the hydrant's side of the street to help firefighters find a hydrant; set by local fire code.
A short sturdy post that guides or blocks vehicles; security bollards are crash-tested to stop trucks.
The domed top of a hydrant; under NFPA 291 it is painted to show the hydrant's flow class.
An iron blade by a doorstep for scraping mud and manure off shoes, dating from the end of the 18th century.
Boston's non-emergency service request system; each report becomes a public ticket routed to a department.
Round ceramic bumps along lane lines that thump under tires, named for Caltrans chemist Elbert Dysart Botts; California is phasing them out.
The three-line arrow that became the mark of the Board of Ordnance by 1597 and appears on OS benchmarks.
A dashed line meaning crossing is permitted; the US standard is 10-foot segments with 30-foot gaps.
Boston's water and sewer utility, created in 1977; its initials are on Boston water and sewer covers.
A street drain with a sump below the outlet pipe where sand and debris settle out.
The line separating traffic going in opposite directions; yellow in the US, usually white in continental Europe.
A cone, drum or barricade used to guide traffic through a work zone.
An optional typeface for light-on-dark US guide signs, approved in 2004, terminated in 2016 and reinstated in 2018.
A small pavement opening, usually 30-36 cm across, where coal was tipped into a vault under the sidewalk.
A small naturally rounded stone used as paving, in New York until about 1860.
In California, a curb painted red, yellow, white, green or blue to signal a parking rule under Vehicle Code 21458.
The clear vertical band, commonly about 40 inches, required by NESC Rules 235C and 238 between power above and communication cables below.
A crosswalk of wide white bars running parallel to traffic.
A company name and often a year pressed into fresh concrete, useful for dating a sidewalk panel.
UK tactile paving of rounded bars across the path meaning hazard, proceed with caution, as at steps.
The X-shaped sign that marks a railroad grade crossing itself.
A vertical cast-iron pipe, capped with a small round 'WATER' lid, reaching 4-6 ft down to a building's water shutoff.
A short slope through a curb that lets wheelchair, stroller and cart users get between sidewalk and street.
The underground shutoff valve on a building's water service line, turned with a long key through the curb box.
A UK Ordnance Survey height mark chiseled as a horizontal line over an upward three-line arrow.
The NGS record for a mark, giving its coordinates, elevation and a station description with directions.
A textured panel, usually truncated domes, that tells blind pedestrians they are about to enter a street or reach a drop-off.
The one-call center for Massachusetts, Maine, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont.
Germany's standard typeface for road signs, standardized in 1936 and required on the Autobahn from 1938.
CGA's annual report on reported damage to buried utilities; 196,977 damages were counted for 2024.
Shorter, closer dashes than a broken line, used to extend a line through an intersection or mark a lane drop.
A cold-climate hydrant whose valve sits below the frost line and whose barrel drains after use so it cannot freeze.
An inset patch of matching stone used to repair damaged granite, required for curb repairs on Beacon Hill.
A solid line marking the side of the road: white on the right, yellow on the left of one-way roads and divided highways (US).

aka: Edison Electric Illuminating Co. of Boston
definition: Boston electric company founded in 1886, predecessor of Boston Edison, NSTAR and Eversource.
The MUTCD sign with a blue circle on a white square reading EVACUATION ROUTE.
The tsunami version of EM-1, with a tsunami symbol and a required blue arrow sign below.
A system in which a detector on the signal responds to a high-rate coded strobe or GPS data to request a green.
A forgery-resistant typeface designed by Karlgeorg Hoefer, used on German license plates since 1994.
A street box that telegraphs its number to the fire alarm office when pulled, using clockwork and dedicated wires.
A dedicated wired network that sends a coded box number from a street box to fire dispatch; Boston's was switched on in 1852.
Inlets on a building where a fire engine pumps water into the sprinkler or standpipe system.
A valve on the water main at the curb that firefighters open with a hydrant wrench to supply hoses and engines.
A marked lane kept clear for fire apparatus, signed NO PARKING FIRE LANE in red on white under the IFC.
An old name for a hydrant, from the wooden plugs hammered into holes bored in hollow-log water mains.
A worker who directs traffic with a STOP/SLOW paddle, wearing ANSI/ISEA 107 Class 2 garments by day and Class 3 at night.
A left-turn indication meaning a permissive turn: turn only after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.
A bright background color required for school warning signs and allowed for pedestrian, bicycle and playground warnings.
A metal Ordnance Survey benchmark plate about 6 by 3 in. set into a wall or trig pillar.
A fuse holder mounted high on a pole near transformers or along primary lines; its fuse melts on unsafe current and the barrel swings open with a loud crack.
A street lantern that burns natural gas around the clock; Boston has about 2,800.
The bell-shaped device beside a gas meter that lowers line pressure to about 0.25 psi for appliances, with a vent that must stay clear.
A faded hand-painted advertisement on a building wall, often uncovered when a later building or billboard comes down.
An enthusiast who photographs or studies utility covers.
A shallow box in an underground conduit run where cable is pulled and spliced, often labeled 'TRAFFIC SIGNAL'.
The government typeface used on most US road signs, first published in 1948, in Series B through F plus E(Modified).
A UK sign with a black H on yellow giving the main diameter (top, mm) and distance to the hydrant cover (bottom, m).
The tool with a pentagonal socket used to open hydrants and their caps.
The German red-bordered hydrant sign giving pipe size and the hydrant's offset from the sign in meters.
A temporary sign with a fluorescent pink background used at crashes and emergencies.
A wire loop saw-cut into the pavement whose inductance changes when a vehicle is above it.
FHWA permission for agencies to use a device or practice not yet in the MUTCD, such as IA-5 for Clearview.
The red, white and blue marker adopted by AASHO on August 14, 1957, a registered trademark since 1967.
British name for a shallow telecom box where cables are spliced; GPO joint box covers date from 1904.
A wall-mounted steel vault holding building keys that only the local fire department can open.
A crosswalk combining two transverse lines with bars between them.
A white line separating lanes of traffic going the same direction (US).
Paint, flags, stakes or whiskers placed by a utility's locator to show the approximate path of a buried line.
The once-per-second tick, no longer than 0.15 seconds, that helps pedestrians find an APS push button.
A crash rating meaning a bollard stopped a 15,000 lb test truck at 50 mph.
Rearranging existing cables on a pole to make room for a new attachment.
A vertical shaft big enough for a worker to climb down to reach underground pipes or cables; modern openings must fit a worker wearing breathing apparatus.
A collectible card showing one Japanese municipality's sewer cover design, issued by the Sewerage PR Platform (GKP) since April 2016.
A fire alarm box connected to a building's own alarm system so it signals the fire department automatically.
A narrow pipe for sampling groundwater or soil vapor, capped with a small bolted lid; triangular lids follow the API 1615 design so drivers won't pour fuel in.

aka: Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices
definition: The federal manual that sets US rules for road signs, signals and markings; the 11th edition took effect January 18, 2024.
The US code that sets clearances on utility poles, including the communication worker safety zone.
The National Fire Protection Association's voluntary recommended practice for flow testing and color-coding hydrants.
NO plus an owner's identifier in its color, meaning that owner has nothing in the dig area.
A mark placed to one side of a buried line with a direction and distance, labeled OFF, when a mark cannot go directly over it.
The organization, such as Dig Safe, that takes dig notices and passes them to member utilities.
Shephard Taylor's term for coal-hole covers, coined in the 1860s.
The datum that Ordnance Survey benchmark heights are measured from.
A large locked box on a concrete pad that steps down electric voltage; usually unvented, with a DANGER sticker.
A ghost sign where layers of older lettering show through each other.
The British specification for detecting, verifying and locating buried utilities, first published in 2014 and revised in 2022.
A dark-until-pushed signal with two reds over a yellow, used only with a marked crosswalk.
The long sideways triangle, sign W14-3, placed on the left side of the road to mark a no-passing zone.
The five-sided operating nut on a hydrant, shaped so ordinary wrenches will not fit and only a hydrant wrench will.
The twist-on device on top of a streetlight that plugs into an ANSI C136.41 receptacle and switches the light.
The six-character identifier for a mark in the National Geodetic Survey database.
A standard surveyor's nail driven into pavement as a control or reference point; the MAG nail is a common alternative.
A small sign mounted under another sign to add information, such as an advisory speed; its code ends in P.
The burned-in or plated mark on a wood pole showing class and height, owner, manufacturer, species, treatment, batch and date.
Light lettering on a dark background, such as white on green.
A post near a building with an OPEN or SHUT window that operates the underground valve on the sprinkler supply.
A right to cross land gained through long public use, which owners block with posted notices such as California's Section 1008 signs.
The medium-voltage power lines at the top of a utility pole, above the communication worker safety zone.
In Boston, a street the city has not accepted as public, where abutters handle maintenance, snow and parking.
An iron rod or pipe at a property corner, often capped with the land surveyor's name and license number.
The US Access Board's design rules for sidewalks, crossings and curb ramps, published August 8, 2023, enforceable once DOJ and DOT adopt them.
A street on which the city handles maintenance, cleaning, plowing and city-owned streetlights.
A UK signalized crossing with no flashing amber, sensors that detect pedestrians, and the signal on the button box.
A US toll plaza approach lane reserved for vehicles with registered electronic toll accounts.
A small reflector or bump fixed to the road that matches the color of its line; the wrong-way side may be red.
Two push-activated rectangular yellow LED lights under a crosswalk sign that flash in an alternating high-frequency pattern.
A small blue light that turns on with the red so police can see red-light violations; it does not use automated photography.
A small sign showing distance along a route, the D10-1 series, counting up from the south or west state line.
A disk near a main station with an arrow pointing back to it, used to recover the station.
French name for a street utility or sewer cover, as seen in Paris.
A sign surface's ability to return headlight light toward the driver; US agencies must keep signs above set minimums.
Grooves or raised bars in the pavement that make noise and vibration when tires cross them.
A rumble strip with the retroreflective edge or center line painted into it.
A heavier Highway Gothic created in 1949-1950 to fit button reflectors, used on freeway guide signs.
A quarried, roughly rectangular paving stone, usually granite, often mistakenly called a cobblestone.
A bike symbol with two chevrons showing where cyclists should ride in a lane shared with cars; added to the MUTCD in 2009.
Japanese for fire hydrant: 消火 'extinguishing fire' plus 栓 'plug or valve'.
The alphanumeric code given to each standard US sign, such as W14-3 for No Passing Zone; a trailing P marks a plaque.
A label on the back of a sign recording materials and fabrication and installation dates; TxDOT uses a punch-coded grid.
A low-power cellular antenna, usually shrouded at the top of a 30-40 ft pole with a cabinet and electric meter below.
A posted Boston street where parking is banned, with ticket and tow, during a declared snow emergency.
A rack that holds a stretched coil of spare fiber cable on a span so each end can later reach a splicing truck on the ground.
An object left to claim a shoveled parking space; tolerated in Boston only during a declared snow emergency and for 48 hours after.
A sealed housing on an aerial cable that protects the point where cables are joined.
A vertical pipe in a building with hose outlets on each floor, fed through an FDC marked STANDPIPE.
The largest outlet on a US hydrant, used by a pumper engine to take its supply.
A solid white line across the lane, 12 to 24 inches wide in the US, showing where to stop.
A curbside disc or stencil warning that the drain carries untreated runoff to a waterway.
A public pull-handle fire alarm box on a pedestal or pole, carrying a number that identifies its location.
The corner sign naming a street; US rules require mixed-case lettering, minimum letter heights and one of four color schemes.
A Boston permit reserving curb space, for example for a move, that comes with cardboard City of Boston No Parking signs.
The low chamber of a catch basin where sediment collects; cleaned before it is 60% full.
The bumpy panel at the foot of a curb ramp; pale yellow in Boston, brick red on historic brick sidewalks.
An electric sensor that signals an alarm if a sprinkler control valve is moved off open.
A smaller, often vented box where phone, cable or fiber lines branch out.
Japanese tactile paving invented by Seiichi Miyake in 1965; dot blocks warn and bar blocks guide.
A marking material melted onto the road in a thick layer; lasts several years but can be scraped off by plows.
The record of a dig request, with a start time and an expiry date; in Massachusetts it lasts 30 days.
The width of a facility plus 18 in. on either side, where excavators avoid machine digging under CGA practice.
A UK signalized crossing shared by pedestrians and cyclists.
The lettering on UK road signs, designed by Jock Kinneir and Margaret Calvert between 1957 and 1963.
A walkable cast-iron grille around a street tree that lets water reach the roots.
A survey mark with a known horizontal position, shown by an inscribed triangle on the disk.
A flat-topped bump 0.2 in (5.1 mm) high, set in rows on US detectable warning panels.

aka: Traffic Signs Regulations and General Directions
definition: The UK legal rulebook for traffic signs, first issued in 1964.
A box at the side of an intersection where cyclists pause to make a left turn in two steps.
A barricade at least 5 ft tall with 3 or 6 striped faces, used for extended road closures.
The legal crosswalk that exists at an intersection leg whether or not it is painted, in most US states.
Glass lenses or prisms set in a sidewalk panel to light the vault below; patented by Thaddeus Hyatt in 1845.
A manhole cover with slots or holes that let smoke and gas escape instead of building up to an explosion.
A fixed-focus camera on a signal structure that watches predefined zones and places a call to the controller.

aka: Vienna Convention on Road Signs and Signals
definition: A 1968 UN treaty standardizing sign shapes, colors and symbols, in force since 1978 with 71 parties as of September 2024.
A sprinkler supply valve operated from the building wall, allowed by NFPA 24 as an alternative to a PIV since 2010.
A sign alerting drivers to a hazard ahead, generally a diamond with a black legend on yellow in the US.
An outdoor sprinkler alarm bell driven by the flowing water itself, needing no electricity.
A warm-climate hydrant that stays full of water, with a separate valve for each outlet.
Tufts of colored plastic strands driven into the ground as a locate or premark.
Outlining a planned dig area in white paint, flags or stakes before requesting locates.
A line at least twice the normal 4 to 6 inch width, used for emphasis.
Machine-cut brick with crisp edges that Boston uses to rebuild historic brick sidewalks with a smoother surface.
The 1963 UK committee report that produced Britain's modern road sign system, law from 1 January 1965.
A mark pressed into concrete by Works Progress Administration crews, with dated examples from 1936 to 1940.
A row of white triangles pointing toward approaching drivers, showing where to yield.
A UK pedestrian crossing with black-and-white stripes and Belisha beacons where drivers must give way to pedestrians.
